710266.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pénkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. Cognates include Sanskrit पञ्च (páñca), Latin quīnque, Old Armenian հինգ (hing) and Old English fīf (English five).

710221.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydʰeti Proto-Hellenic *péitʰō Ancient Greek πείθω From Proto-Hellenic *péitʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-.

710270.t: From Proto-Indo-European *penkʷēḱomth₂, from earlier *pénkʷedḱomt (“fifty”). Cognates include Latin quīnquāgintā, Sanskrit पञ्चाशत् (pañcāśát) and Old Armenian յիսուն (yisun).

710285.t: From Proto-Indo-European *peri (“in crossing; in passing”), locative singular of *per- (“before; in front”). Cognates include Sanskrit परि॑ (pári), Latin per, Lithuanian per, English for, and Albanian për.

710206.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pəkʰús, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰénǵʰus (“thick”), from *bʰenǵʰ- (“thick; to swell”). Cognates include Sanskrit बहु (bahú, “much, many”) and Avestan 𐬠𐬄𐬰𐬀𐬵 (bązah).

710277.t: According to Sihler, the term is a back-formation from ἔπεψα (épepsa) and πέψω (pépsō), the aorist and future forms of πέσσω (péssō).

710284.t: Traditionally explained (such as by Frisk) as a derivative from πέρδομαι (pérdomai, “to fart”), due to the droning sound when partridges take wing.

710231.t: Uncertain. Some suggest the source is Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”), whereas others such as Beekes suggest a non-Indo-European origin.

710239.t: According to Beekes, from Proto-Indo-European *pélmn̥, from *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *felmô (“covering, skin”) (whence English film).

710229.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂ Proto-Indo-European *périh₂ Proto-Hellenic *péřřa Ancient Greek πεῖρα (peîră) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂…

710215.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“trace, footstep”), and related to πούς (poús, “foot”). Compare πέδον (pédon, “soil, ground”).

710203.t: From earlier *πάκσνα (*páksnā), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-, like πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “I fasten”).

710253.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷendʰ-; cognate with πάθος (páthos) and πάσχω (páskhō).

710237.t: Uncertain: Compare Sanskrit परशु (paraśú, “axe”) and Ossetian фӕрӕт (færæt, “axe”), pointing to a late, dialectal Proto-Indo-European word like *peleḱu- which does not appear to be a native formation.

710224.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *per- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂ Proto-Indo-European *périh₂ Proto-Hellenic *péřřa Ancient Greek πεῖρα From Proto-Hellenic *péřřa, from Proto-Indo-European *pér-ih₂ ~…

710232.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pélas, from Proto-Indo-European *pélh₂-s, from *pelh₂- (“to approach”).

710281.t: Perhaps akin to πείρω (peírō, “to pierce, to run through”) or περάω (peráō, “to drive right through”), see also πέρα (péra) and πέραν (péran), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to pierce”).

710219.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ped͏̌d͏̌ós, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yo-s (“foot”); see also πούς (poús).

710250.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-er-os, from *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”) and formally almost completely agreeing with Lithuanian beñdras (“common, shared”); compare also Sanskrit बन्धु (bandhu, “relative, kindred”).

710259.t: From πέντε (pénte, “five”) + -άκις (-ắkĭs, suffix for adverb of repetition).

710278.t: From Proto-Indo-European *pékʷonts (“cooking, ripening”); related to πέσσω (péssō, “to soften, ripen”).

710244.t: By surface analysis, πέσσω (péssō, “to cook, to bake”) + -μα (-ma). According to Beekes, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷ-mn̥, itself from *pekʷ-.

710242.t: Perhaps a loanword from Thracian considering the origin of this type of shield. Usually connected with Latin pellis (“skin”) and Ancient Greek πέλμα (pélma, “sole of the foot”), so from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover”).

710256.t: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)penh₁- (“to weave, spin”), with semantic shift "to weave, stretch" > "to tense, strain" > "to exert oneself".

710210.t: From Proto-Indo-European *pṓds, like πέδον (pédon) and πέζα (péza). The same semantics are found in Latin pedica (“shackle”), impediō (“to hinder”) and Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”).

710234.t: Derived from πέλεκυς (pélekus, “axe”), because of the functional and/or formal similarity with an axe.

710283.t: From περάω (peráō, “to cross, pass over”) (from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to cross, go beyond”)) + -της (-tēs). Unrelated to πειρατής (peiratḗs, “pirate”), despite similarity in form.

710272.t: From πεντήκοντα (pentḗkonta) + ἀρχός (arkhós), literally “commander of fifty”.
